title: ABA Formal Opinion 512: Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools
author: ABA Standing Committee on Ethics and Professional Responsibility

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The opinion accepts the cluster’s core view that generative AI is useful for selected legal tasks but remains fallible, context-dependent and subject to lawyer verification and accountability. It materially develops that proposition by translating it into concrete Model Rules duties covering competence, confidentiality, client communication, court submissions, supervision, vendor diligence and fees.
qs: In short, regardless of the level of review the lawyer selects, the lawyer is fully responsible for the work on behalf of the client.

st.t: AI filings: Disclosure rules divide otherwise similar courts
st.an: ABA Opinion 512 supports conditional AI assistance while retaining lawyers’ professional responsibility. It frames generative AI use through existing duties of competence, confidentiality, communication, supervision, candour, meritorious advocacy and reasonable fees, while recognising potential efficiency and quality benefits. The supplied excerpt does not materially address courts’ divergent disclosure, certification or prohibition rules, or provide detailed verification standards.
qs: Introduction          Many lawyers use artificial intelligence (AI) based technologies in their practices to improve the efficiency and quality of legal services to clients.1 A well-known use is electronic discovery in litigation, in which lawyers use technology-assisted review to categorize vast quantities of documents as responsive or non-responsive and to segregate privileged documents.

st.t: Generative automation: Fluent work product still needs authority
st.an: The opinion supports the cluster’s core framing by identifying generative AI as a probabilistic text-generation tool that can produce substantive legal work across research, review and drafting. It also places use within professional-conduct duties, though the supplied excerpt raises competence, confidentiality and disclosure questions rather than specifying verification or supervision requirements.
qs: GAI tools may assist lawyers in tasks such as legal research, contract review, due diligence, document review, regulatory compliance, and drafting letters, contracts, briefs, and other legal documents.

Formal Opinion 512                                                                                                  2         GAI tools—whether general purpose or designed specifically for the practice of law—raise important questions under the ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct.3 What level of competency should lawyers acquire regarding a GAI tool?

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: The opinion supports the cluster’s copilot framing: generative AI may assist across legal tasks, but its probabilistic output can be false or fabricated, making uncritical reliance professionally hazardous. It also reinforces human responsibility through competence, confidentiality and disclosure concerns, though the supplied excerpts do not assess verification costs or provide comparative evidence on speed, cost or quality.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The opinion supports the cluster’s supervised, task-bounded framing: it recognizes AI’s efficiency and quality uses in established legal workflows while keeping lawyers responsible for competence, confidentiality, supervision, candor and other professional duties. It does not directly address apprenticeship, labour-market or pricing risks.

st.t: Professional governance: Existing duties need active AI scrutiny
st.an: ABA Formal Opinion 512 directly supports the cluster’s core proposition that generative AI use remains governed by existing professional duties and requires lawyers to actively consider those obligations to protect clients. The supplied excerpt identifies the relevant duties but does not materially extend the cluster’s account with detailed verification or implementation procedures.

st.t: Sanctions evidence: Fabrication signal supports little regulation
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s conclusion that the supplied material is insufficient for substantive ethical or regulatory analysis: it contains only a copyright notice and no claims from ABA Formal Opinion 512. It does not address or add evidence concerning sanctions for fabricated AI-generated citations.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The opinion directly supports the cluster’s supervised-AI framework: lawyers retain professional judgment and full accountability, while verification is required but calibrated to the particular tool and task. It also supports continuing competence, confidentiality controls, institutional supervision and honest billing rather than autonomous reliance on AI.
qs: While GAI may be used as a springboard or foundation for legal work—for example, by generating an analysis on which a lawyer bases legal advice, or by generating a draft from which a lawyer produces a legal document—lawyers may not abdicate their responsibilities by relying solely on a GAI tool to perform tasks that call for the exercise of professional judgment.

The appropriate amount of independent verification or review required to satisfy Rule 1.1 will necessarily depend on the GAI tool and the specific task that it performs as part of the lawyer’s representation of a client.

st.t: Supervisory accountability: Verification must test substantive support
st.an: ABA Opinion 512 directly supports the cluster’s core proposition: lawyers retain professional judgment and responsibility when using generative AI, while the required independent verification is proportionate to the particular tool and task rather than necessarily duplicating all automated work. It provides foundational support, though it does not itself develop the cluster’s broader extension to judicial and institutional leadership accountability.

kp.k: Existing professional duties govern generative AI use
kp.d: The ABA Standing Committee offers general ethical guidance under the ABA Model Rules as amended through August 2023, rather than reporting new empirical research. Its July 29, 2024 opinion applies existing duties to GAI and anticipates updated guidance as tools develop.
qs: This Opinion identifies some ethical issues involving the use of GAI tools and offers general guidance for lawyers attempting to navigate this emerging landscape.

It is anticipated that this Committee and state and local bar association ethics committees will likely offer updated guidance on professional conduct issues relevant to specific GAI tools as they develop.

kp.k: GAI offers broad task assistance, not autonomous professional judgment
kp.d: The Committee describes potential efficiency and quality gains across research, review, compliance and drafting. It frames GAI as assistance or a foundation for lawyers' work, not a replacement for personal judgment in advice, negotiation or other professional functions.
qs: GAI tools may assist lawyers in tasks such as legal research, contract review, due diligence, document review, regulatory compliance, and drafting letters, contracts, briefs, and other legal documents.

For example, lawyers may not leave it to GAI tools alone to offer legal advice to clients, negotiate clients’ claims, or perform other functions that require a lawyer’s personal judgment or participation.

kp.k: Technological competence requires continuing, tool-specific understanding
kp.d: Under Rule 1.1, lawyers need a reasonable understanding of their particular tools' capabilities, limitations, benefits and risks, not specialist GAI expertise. They may acquire that understanding themselves or consult competent colleagues and experts, but must keep it current as technology evolves.
qs: To competently use a GAI tool in a client representation, lawyers need not become GAI experts.
Given the fast-paced evolution of GAI tools, technological competence presupposes that lawyers remain vigilant about the tools’ benefits and risks.

kp.k: Unreliable output creates competence and misrepresentation risks
kp.d: The opinion warns that limited, outdated or biased training data can produce unreliable, incomplete or discriminatory results, while fabricated output can mislead clients, courts and third parties. As external evidence, footnote 14 cites Magesh and colleagues' Stanford study dated June 26, 2024, reporting hallucinations in leading legal research companies' GAI systems between 17% and 33% of the time; this is a cited study result, not an ABA measurement.
qs: If the quality, breadth, and sources of the underlying data on which a GAI tool is trained are limited or outdated or reflect biased content, the tool might produce unreliable, incomplete, or discriminatory results.
hallucinate between 17% and 33% of the time

Because GAI tools are subject to mistakes, lawyers’ uncritical reliance on content created by a GAI tool can result in inaccurate legal advice to clients or misleading representations to courts and third parties.

kp.k: Verification varies by task; lawyer responsibility remains
kp.d: The required independent verification or review depends on the tool and task. The Committee's contract-summary example permits reliance without manually reviewing every document where earlier manual testing of a smaller subset established accuracy. Prior experience and discrete legal tasks may justify less review, but do not transfer responsibility away from the lawyer.
qs: The appropriate amount of independent verification or review required to satisfy Rule 1.1 will necessarily depend on the GAI tool and the specific task that it performs as part of the lawyer’s representation of a client.
In short, regardless of the level of review the lawyer selects, the lawyer is fully responsible for the work on behalf of the client.

kp.k: Future competence standards could eventually require GAI
kp.d: The Committee presents mandatory use for certain tasks as a possibility, not a current general requirement. It conditions that prospect on professional acceptance, reliable results, financial availability and client demand. For now, lawyers should know relevant tools sufficiently to make informed, client-centered choices; unreasonable-fee constraints and market forces may favor more efficient methods.
qs: As GAI tools continue to develop and become more widely available, it is conceivable that lawyers will eventually have to use them to competently complete certain tasks for clients.

The establishment of such an expectation would likely require an increased acceptance of GAI tools across the legal profession, a track record of reliable results from those platforms, the widespread availability of these technologies to lawyers from a cost or financial standpoint, and robust client demand for GAI tools as an efficiency or cost-cutting measure.

kp.k: Confidentiality requires fact-specific assessment before entering client information
kp.d: Rule 1.6 protects all information relating to representation, regardless of source, with similar protections for former and prospective clients under Rules 1.9(c) and 1.18(b). Before inputting information, lawyers must assess outside access and inappropriate internal access or use, considering sensitivity, safeguards, client, matter, task and tool. The opinion recommends understanding contractual terms and privacy policies, with expert assistance where needed.
qs: Before lawyers input information relating to the representation of a client into a GAI tool, they must evaluate the risks that the information will be disclosed to or accessed by others outside the firm.

As a baseline, all lawyers should read and understand the Terms of Use, privacy policy, and related contractual terms and policies of any GAI tool they use to learn who has access to the information that the lawyer inputs into the tool or consult with a colleague or external expert who has read and analyzed those terms and policies.

kp.k: Self-learning tools can expose information across representations
kp.d: The Committee warns that information entered for one client may later emerge in outputs used for another client, including within the same firm and across ethical walls. Based on capabilities and risks at publication, it requires informed consent before representation information enters self-learning tools whose outputs could disclose it. The opinion expressly allows that technological changes could alter this conclusion.
qs: This can occur when information relating to one client’s representation is input into the tool, then later revealed in response to prompts by lawyers working on other matters, who then share that output with other clients, file it with the court, or otherwise disclose it.

Accordingly, because many of today’s self-learning GAI tools are designed so that their output could lead directly or indirectly to the disclosure of information relating to the representation of a client, a client’s informed consent is required prior to inputting information relating to the representation into such a GAI tool.
As the technology develops, the risks may change in ways that would alter our conclusion.

kp.k: Informed consent requires specific explanations, not boilerplate
kp.d: Where consent is required, lawyers must explain why the tool is used, benefits, specific information exposed, risks of access and potential adverse uses. Generic engagement-letter authorization is insufficient. Conversely, idea generation without inputting representation information does not require informed consent on that confidentiality basis.
qs: To obtain informed consent when using a GAI tool, merely adding general, boiler-plate provisions to engagement letters purporting to authorize the lawyer to use GAI is not sufficient.

As an example, if a lawyer is using the tool for idea generation in a manner that does not require inputting information relating to the representation, client informed consent would not be necessary.

kp.k: Client communication duties extend beyond confidentiality consent
kp.d: Rule 1.4 creates a separate, circumstance-dependent disclosure obligation. Lawyers must disclose GAI use when asked or required by engagement terms or outside counsel guidelines, and consult when it affects fees or significant decisions, such as litigation-outcome assessment or jury selection. Client expectations, retained expertise, task significance and information sensitivity matter; universal disclosure is not required.
qs: Depending on the circumstances, client disclosure may be unnecessary.
Lawyers must also consult clients when the use of a GAI tool is relevant to the basis or reasonableness of a lawyer’s fee.

A client would reasonably want to know whether, in providing advice or making important decisions about how to carry out the representation, the lawyer is exercising independent judgment or, in the alternative, is deferring to the output of a GAI tool.

kp.k: Court submissions require review and correction of AI errors
kp.d: The opinion applies Rules 3.1, 3.3 and 8.4(c) to AI-assisted litigation, identifying nonexistent opinions, inaccurate authority analysis and misleading arguments as problems already encountered. Lawyers must check submissions and correct errors, including omitted controlling authority. Some courts require GAI disclosure, so lawyers should consult applicable local rules.
qs: Issues that have arisen to date with lawyers’ use of GAI outputs include citations to nonexistent opinions, inaccurate analysis of authority, and use of misleading arguments.

In judicial proceedings, duties to the tribunal likewise require lawyers, before submitting materials to a court, to review these outputs, including analysis and citations to authority, and to correct errors, including misstatements of law and fact, a failure to include controlling legal authority, and misleading arguments.

kp.k: Firm leaders must establish policies, supervision and training
kp.d: Under Rules 5.1 and 5.3, managerial lawyers must set permissible-use policies and supervisors must make reasonable efforts to secure compliance by lawyers and nonlawyers. Training should address technology basics, capabilities, limitations, ethical risks, confidentiality and secure data handling. The opinion also suggests marking stored AI-generated materials so later users understand their potential fallibility.
qs: Managerial lawyers must establish clear policies regarding the law firm’s permissible use of GAI, and supervisory lawyers must make reasonable efforts to ensure that the firm’s lawyers and nonlawyers comply with their professional obligations when using GAI tools.

Training could include the basics of GAI technology, the capabilities and limitations of the tools, ethical issues in use of GAI and best practices for secure data handling, privacy, and confidentiality.

kp.k: External GAI provision requires outsourcing-style due diligence
kp.d: The Committee extends earlier outsourcing and cloud-computing guidance to GAI providers and tools. Lawyers should investigate capability, confidentiality, security, hiring and conflicts practices, contractual enforceability and remedies, breach notification, liability limitations, retention and proprietary rights, and cyberattack or service-failure risks.
qs: Earlier opinions recognize that when outsourcing legal and nonlegal services to third-party providers, lawyers must ensure, for example, that the third party will do the work capably and protect the confidentiality of information relating to the representation.
These concepts also apply to GAI providers and tools.

kp.k: Hourly billing must reflect actual work, including verification
kp.d: GAI efficiency cannot justify billing hypothetical hours saved. Lawyers billing hourly may charge actual time entering prompts and reviewing results for accuracy and completeness. The opinion illustrates this with 15 minutes spent entering information for a pleading, plus actual review time. Before charging for GAI tools or services, lawyers must explain the charge basis, preferably in writing.
qs: GAI tools may provide lawyers with a faster and more efficient way to render legal services to their clients, but lawyers who bill clients an hourly rate for time spent on a matter must bill for their actual time.

If a lawyer uses a GAI tool to draft a pleading and expends 15 minutes to input the relevant information into the GAI program, the lawyer may charge for the 15 minutes as well as for the time the lawyer expends to review the resulting draft for accuracy and completeness.

kp.k: Flat and contingent fees remain subject to reasonableness
kp.d: Rule 1.5(a)'s factors apply to flat and contingent arrangements as well as hourly fees. The Committee says substantially faster completion through GAI may make an unchanged flat fee unreasonable; it does not state that every productivity gain requires a proportionate fee reduction.
qs: The factors set forth in Rule 1.5(a) also apply when evaluating the reasonableness of charges for GAI tools when the lawyer and client agree on a flat or contingent fee.

For example, if using a GAI tool enables a lawyer to complete tasks much more quickly than without the tool, it may be unreasonable under Rule 1.5 for the lawyer to charge the same flat fee when using the GAI tool as when not using it.

kp.k: Tool expenses depend on function and advance agreements
kp.d: Routine practice infrastructure, such as a grammar tool within word-processing software, should be treated as overhead absent advance contrary disclosure. Client-specific, per-use contract review ordinarily may be billed at actual out-of-pocket cost. For proprietary in-house tools, firms may agree rates in advance; without agreement, charges are limited to direct costs plus reasonable directly associated expenses, with disclosures and no duplication.
qs: To the extent a particular tool or service functions similarly to equipping and maintaining a legal practice, a lawyer should consider its cost to be overhead and not charge the client for its cost absent a contrary disclosure to the client in advance.

Absent an agreement, the firm may charge the client no more than the direct cost associated with the tool (if any) plus a reasonable allocation of expenses directly associated with providing the GAI tool, while providing appropriate disclosures to the client consistent with Formal Opinion 93-379.
The lawyer must ensure that the amount charged is not duplicative of other charges to this or other clients.

kp.k: Routine AI learning costs cannot be charged to clients
kp.d: Maintaining competence in routinely used GAI is the lawyer's responsibility, and clients cannot be billed for time attributable to the lawyer's inexperience. A limited exception may apply where a client explicitly requests a particular unfamiliar tool for the matter; the parties should first agree the resulting billing terms, preferably memorializing them.
qs: Therefore, a lawyer may not charge a client to learn about how to use a GAI tool or service that the lawyer will regularly use for clients because lawyers must maintain competence in the tools they use, including but not limited to GAI technology.

However, if a client explicitly requests that a specific GAI tool be used in furtherance of the matter and the lawyer is not knowledgeable in using that tool, it may be appropriate for the lawyer to bill the client to gain the knowledge to use the tool effectively.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The ABA Standing Committee describes GAI as a potential efficiency and quality aid, not a replacement for lawyers’ professional judgment, and anticipates possible changes to competence expectations, confidentiality practices, supervision, and billing.
pts.d: In Formal Opinion 512, the Committee states that GAI can assist with research, review, due diligence, compliance, and drafting. It warns that inaccurate, biased, or fabricated output can lead to incorrect advice and misleading court submissions, making appropriate human verification necessary. Lawyers remain responsible for their work and cannot delegate functions requiring personal professional judgment entirely to GAI. The Committee predicts that improved tools could eventually become necessary for competent performance of certain tasks. It also identifies possible disclosure of client information through tools described as self-learning, including across matters within a firm; requires fact-specific risk assessment and, for the risky uses identified, informed consent; and describes circumstances requiring client consultation. Adoption entails firm policies, training, supervision, and provider due diligence. Efficiency gains affect permissible billing: hourly charges must reflect actual time, including review, rather than time that would have been spent without GAI. An unchanged flat fee may become unreasonable when GAI substantially reduces the work, but the opinion does not prescribe an automatic reduction for every flat fee. Tool expenses depend on their characteristics, costs, disclosures, and agreements; ordinary learning costs generally cannot be charged to clients.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The opinion principally offers ethical interpretation and analogies to earlier technologies, supplemented by a cited legal-research hallucination study and examples of problematic outputs.
pts.d: The Committee grounds its conclusions in the ABA Model Rules, earlier ABA opinions on outsourcing, technology, and billing, state and local ethics guidance, judicial decisions, and secondary commentary. These are interpretive authorities rather than new empirical findings. The cited Stanford study by Magesh and colleagues, dated June 26, 2024, is the evidence offered for a 17%–33% hallucination range in leading legal-research GAI systems; this is an attributed study result, not the Committee’s own test or a rate for all GAI tools. Separately, the opinion describes litigation problems involving nonexistent opinions, inaccurate analysis, and misleading arguments, citing DC Bar Opinion 388, without measuring their prevalence. Its efficiency and quality claims are expressed as potential benefits, without quantified productivity evidence. Its prediction about future competence expectations draws on the historical integration of email, electronic documents, and computerized research. Contract-summary testing and the 15-minute pleading example illustrate how obligations might apply, rather than report observed outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The July 29, 2024 opinion distinguishes present obligations from conditional, undated predictions about future adoption and explicitly anticipates changing guidance.
pts.d: The Committee evaluates tools and risks as of publication and expects further guidance as their capabilities develop. It does not say lawyers already must use GAI generally. A future competence expectation would likely depend on professional acceptance, reliable results, affordability and availability, and robust client demand; no date is supplied. Current verification requirements vary with the tool and task, including prior testing or experience. The confidentiality analysis depends on the client, matter, task, and tool. The informed-consent conclusion concerning self-learning tools is expressly tied to current risks and capabilities; idea generation without inputting representation-related information is identified as a use not requiring confidentiality-based consent. Disclosure under the communication duty is also circumstance-dependent, not universal. Billing conclusions depend on actual work, the fee arrangement, reasonableness, and advance disclosures or agreements. Training in a client-requested unfamiliar tool may be billable by agreement, unlike learning a tool the lawyer will regularly use.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The opinion addresses practicing lawyers, firm managers and supervisors, subordinate lawyers and nonlawyers, clients, courts, and outside providers, rather than predicting employment or market-share changes.
pts.d: Lawyers using either general-purpose or legal-specific GAI gain potential assistance but retain responsibility for competence, verification, confidentiality, communication, and reasonable charges. Managers must establish policies; supervisors must ensure appropriate use and training by subordinate lawyers and nonlawyers, with additional obligations when outside providers employ GAI. Clients may receive faster or more economical service while facing risks to information and advice; their instructions, expectations, significant decisions, consent, and fee arrangements constrain use. Confidentiality protections extend to former and prospective clients. Courts and third parties can be affected by false or misleading output, with lawyers required to review submissions and comply with applicable court rules. Firms investing in proprietary tools face constraints on expense recovery. The opinion supplies no prediction about associate displacement, staffing shapes, ALSP market share, or access-to-justice outcomes. Its ethical framework is based on the ABA Model Rules and should not be read as a statement that every jurisdiction has adopted identical requirements.
